text: A clean vendor assessment feels like the finish line, but it isn't. This lesson is about the step that actually makes those findings mean something: writing them into the contract as real, enforceable obligations.

A SIG response that says a vendor encrypts data at rest is just a statement of fact at the moment it was written. It becomes an obligation only when the contract requires it, names the standard, and says what happens if it isn't met. That's the gap between assessing a vendor and governing one, and it's closed with a security addendum attached to the master services agreement.

Four clauses do the real work. Security SLAs pin down encryption standards, patch timelines, and MFA requirements. Breach notification timelines replace "notify us promptly" with a concrete window, commonly 24 to 72 hours, because the customer's own regulatory clock is already running and can't wait on the vendor. Right-to-audit clauses give the customer a contractual hook to verify controls directly. And subcontractor flow-down pushes those same obligations down to the vendor's own subcontractors.

Right-to-audit language is real and standard across the industry — something close to: the customer, or an independent auditor it designates, may audit the vendor's relevant security controls with reasonable notice, no more than once every twelve months, unless an incident or regulation requires more.

Here's the honest part: that clause rarely gets exercised as a literal on-site audit, especially against a large cloud provider, which simply can't let every customer send auditors through its data centers. In practice, annual SOC 2 and ISO evidence satisfies it day to day, with the literal right held in reserve for Tier 1 vendors or triggered after an actual incident. Its value is being a credible fallback, not a constant exercise.

None of this depth belongs on every vendor relationship — it should scale with the tier from Lesson 22, concentrated where sensitive data or system access actually exists. Lesson 24 picks up from here: why a vendor that looked clean at signing can still drift into a very different risk over time.
